metadata.title: Rethinking Item Fairness Using Single World Intervention Graphs

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The empirical application uses TIMSS 2011 mathematics data for U.S. 8th-grade students, restricted to Booklet 1 and to 26 mathematics items, with further exclusions for incomplete item responses and missing values in variables used. The manuscript reports a final analytic sample of 660 respondents after data cleaning, but it does not specify whether TIMSS complex survey weights (e.g., student sampling weights) or replicate weights were applied in the DIF/CDIF analyses. Because the CDIF detection is implemented via parametric outcome regression with covariate adjustment (logistic regression and likelihood-ratio testing), the paper does not document any weight-aware estimation strategy; thus, weighting cannot be confirmed from the provided text. For replication, analysts should verify in the referenced R code or supplementary materials whether TIMSS sampling weights were used and, if not, interpret the results as conditional on the analyzed sample rather than fully population-representative estimates.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variables in the empirical TIMSS application are dichotomized item responses (correct vs. incorrect) for a single item (M032595), rather than PV-based cognitive achievement scores. Because the analysis targets item-level response probabilities and uses covariate adjustment (e.g., BSDGHER) under a SWIG-based identification argument, plausible values are not applicable to the outcome as modeled. The manuscript does not report a specific missing-data handling method beyond describing data cleaning exclusions (e.g., excluding students with missing values in variables used), so the exact missing-data strategy for all variables is not fully documented.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: For the TIMSS application, the authors use TIMSS 2011 mathematics assessment data for U.S. 8th-grade students and restrict to students who received Booklet 1 containing 26 mathematics items. They select 19 DIF-free items as anchor items using the regularized DIF detection method of Lyu et al. (2025) to estimate students’ math ability scores, then analyze a single target item labeled M032595. The final analytic sample consists of 660 respondents after data cleaning, excluding students who did not complete all items, did not answer all items correctly or incorrectly (i.e., incomplete response patterns), or had missing values in variables used.

main_findings.dataset_used: TIMSS 2011 Grade 8 Mathematics (U.S., Booklet 1; item M032595)
main_findings.target_variable: CDIF for item M032595 (binary item response)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Reg Adj (CDIF) p-value: 0.088 (no CDIF); Traditional DIF: Std p-value 0.100 (DIF), MH p-value 0.003 (DIF), Logistic p-value 0.010 (DIF).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2011 Grade 8 Mathematics data (U.S., Booklet 1; item M032595), the study leveraged sex and home educational resources to model item response under the SWIG-based CDIF identification strategy, finding that the regression-adjusted CDIF test yielded no CDIF (p = 0.088) while traditional DIF methods flagged DIF (e.g., MH p = 0.003; Logistic p = 0.010). This indicates that, after adjusting for the assumed confounding pathway via home educational resources, the observed sex-related response differences are not interpreted as causally unfair item functioning under the authors’ SWIG assumptions.

data.outcome_summary: The article proposes a causal framework for differential item functioning (CDIF) using Single-World Intervention Graphs (SWIGs), and it demonstrates the approach with both simulations and an empirical TIMSS application. In the TIMSS 2011 Grade 8 mathematics analysis, the authors restrict to U.S. students who received Booklet 1, use 19 DIF-free items as anchor items to estimate math ability, and then analyze a single dichotomous item response (M032595). For the protected variable sex (ITSEX), traditional DIF methods (standardized D-statistic, Mantel–Haenszel, and logistic regression) flag DIF in favor of boys, but the SWIG-informed regression-adjusted CDIF approach finds no CDIF after adjusting for home educational resources (BSDGHER), reporting p = 0.088. The key limitation is that the causal conclusion depends on the correctness of the assumed SWIG and measured confounders; unmeasured confounding could still bias CDIF estimates.
